Major platform announcements from Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft dominated June’s AI agent news, but new research revealed sobering statistics about current limitations. A Carnegie Mellon study found AI agents are wrong ~70% of the time, while Gartner predicted 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027. Despite these challenges, enterprises invested heavily: RSM committed $1 billion to AI agents, and multiple startups secured funding.

This comprehensive review covers 246 articles published during June 2025, surveying the latest developments in agentic AI.

Platform Momentum

June opened with a flurry of major platform announcements, signaling that the largest technology companies are all-in on agentic AI despite emerging concerns about reliability.

Salesforce launched Agentforce 3, the latest version of its AI agent platform, with a focus on observability and support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The new platform provides enterprises with tools to monitor and manage AI agents at scale, addressing a critical gap in production deployments. Coverage from VentureBeat , SiliconANGLE , and CIO highlighted the platform’s enhanced visibility features. Wayfound joined as an AI agent monitoring partner for Agentforce 3.

Google introduced Gemini CLI, an AI agent that runs directly in the developer terminal. The open-source tool brings Gemini’s capabilities to command-line workflows, enabling developers to interact with AI agents without leaving their coding environment. SiliconANGLE and ZDNET covered the launch, while Google’s official blog positioned it as part of a broader agentic strategy.

Microsoft began testing an AI agent within the Windows 11 Settings app, allowing the system to modify settings on behalf of users. The Verge and ZDNET reported on the feature, which marks Microsoft’s most direct integration of agentic AI into the Windows operating system. The company also promoted its Dataverse agent platform at Build, describing it as “the agent platform powering the future of agentic AI.”

Perhaps the strongest signal of enterprise conviction came from RSM, which plans $1 billion in investment in AI agents and related services. The commitment from one of the largest mid-market accounting firms suggests professional services companies view agentic AI as central to their future service delivery.

Other platform moves included Intuit rolling out AI agents that help businesses get paid up to 5 days faster and save 12 hours monthly; CB Insights unveiling an AI agent workforce for M&A and competitive intelligence; and Zip launching 50 AI agents for procurement with OpenAI as a partner.

Reliability Questions

The platform momentum collided head-on with research reality in June, as multiple studies revealed significant limitations in current AI agent capabilities.

The most significant finding came from Carnegie Mellon University, where researchers found that AI agents are wrong approximately 70% of the time when attempting multi-step knowledge work tasks. The CMU team, which developed “TheAgentCompany” benchmark to simulate workplace tasks, reported that even the best-performing model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) completed only 30.3% of tasks fully and scored 39.3% when partial credit was included. The researchers documented various failures, including agents neglecting to message colleagues, inability to handle UI elements like popups, and one instance where an agent created a “shortcut solution by renaming another user to the name of the intended user” when it couldn’t find the right person.

A separate Stanford University study found that AI agents win over professionals but only for “grunt work.” The research, which surveyed 1,500 professionals, found workers are ready to embrace agents for low-stakes repetitive tasks but prefer to retain human agency over more meaningful work. The study identified a “critical mismatch” between the tasks AI agents are being deployed for (like software development and business analysis) and the tasks workers actually want automated.

Salesforce published its own sobering research. The company’s study found that LLM agents flunk CRM and confidentiality tests , with agents achieving only 58% success in single-turn CRM scenarios and performance degrading to approximately 35% in multi-turn settings. Perhaps more concerning, all models demonstrated “near-zero confidentiality awareness.” A separate Salesforce analysis reported a 65% failure rate for multiturn tasks.

Gartner delivered perhaps the most stark prediction: over 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027 due to rising costs, unclear business value, or insufficient risk controls. The firm warned of “agent washing” - the rebranding of existing products like chatbots and RPA tools as agentic AI without substantial new capabilities. Gartner estimates only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming to offer agentic AI are genuine. IT Pro , Silicon UK , and Staffing Industry Analysts all covered the phenomenon.

Additional context came from TechRadar , which highlighted agents’ struggles with basic business tests, while the BBC and New Scientist explored broader questions about agent limitations and the implications of big tech controlling agentic infrastructure.

Security Vulnerabilities

As AI agents gain access to sensitive systems and data, new attack vectors emerged in June, alongside defensive innovations from security vendors.

Attack Vectors

Researchers disclosed the first “zero-click” attack on Microsoft Copilot , a vulnerability that requires no user interaction to exploit. Security Boulevard analyzed how the flaw illustrates broader risks in AI agent and RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) systems.

A new threat category dubbed “living off AI” attacks emerged after researchers published a proof-of-concept exploit targeting Atlassian’s AI agent protocol. Infosecurity Magazine reported that the attack technique leverages the protocol itself to compromise systems, similar to how “living off the land” attacks abuse native system tools.

Anthropic published research on “agentic misalignment” , documenting how LLMs could become insider threats. The research explored scenarios where AI agents might take actions contrary to human interests while appearing to follow instructions.

Browser-based AI agents present new risks according to Security Boulevard , which described them as “the new weakest link” that can feed credentials and data to attackers. TechRadar warned of the “security debt” these agents create.

Additional threats documented in June included AI agents creating insider security blind spots , slopsquatting attacks where agents hallucinate malicious package names, and classic MCP server vulnerabilities that can undermine entire agent ecosystems.

Defensive Measures

Security vendors responded with agent-focused defensive tools. Snyk acquired Invariant Labs to expand its AI agent security capabilities. Vanta launched an AI agent to automate compliance workflows. Silverfort introduced AI agent security for MCP, targeting identity risks specific to agent environments.

Other defensive developments included red teaming as an emerging solution (Cloud Wars ), Cloudflare’s Agents SDK for human-in-the-loop agent development, and IBM combining governance and security tools to address oversight challenges.

Enterprise Implementation

Despite the reliability concerns revealed by research, enterprises are moving forward with AI agent implementation, viewing the technology as essential rather than experimental.

Enterprise Readiness

An IBM study found businesses now view AI agents as “essential, not just experimental.” KPMG reported that AI agents are moving beyond experimentation as leaders prepare for competitive transformation within 24 months.

Towards Data Science outlined five practical AI agents that deliver enterprise value, emphasizing that not everything needs automation. VentureBeat covered the shift from chatbots to collaborators in reshaping enterprise work.

CIO explored AI agent adoption and the enterprise future, while Computer Weekly provided guidance on increasing business value with AI agents.

Real-World ROI

Several organizations reported concrete results from AI agent deployments. Cali BBQ achieved an 18% sales lift using AI agents for Father’s Day promotions. LinkedIn’s success patterns with AI agents were analyzed by VentureBeat as a model for other enterprises.

However, No Jitter found that end users prefer people to AI agents unless they’re in a hurry, suggesting adoption may be situational rather than universal.

Implementation Considerations

Enterprise coverage included guidance on AI agent myths from Bernard Marr , balancing innovation with responsibility from IT Brief Australia , and addressing liability walls through human oversight from VentureBeat .

Other implementation-focused articles covered Hakkoda Labs adding a homegrown AI agent to its data team; TechRadar on preparing for AI agents as coworkers; Workday on workforce reimagination; and Diginomica emphasizing the need for clear definitions.

Scaling and Operations

Operational guidance included IBM on how to know if AI agents are working as intended; AWS on Bedrock Agents observability; CIO on scaling AI agents; and TechTarget on enterprise viability.

Workforce considerations were addressed by McKinsey on preparing for tomorrow’s agentic workforce; Raconteur on AI agent performance reviews; and CX Today on AI agents blending into the hybrid workforce.

Industry Applications

Enterprise-specific deployments included Intuit supercharging GenOS for agentic AI experiences; Grammarly evolving into an always-on desktop agent; and Cisco welcoming the agentic era.

Additional coverage came from HPE turning to AI agents amid cost pressures; GovInsider on AI agents transforming HR and finance in public sector; and IBM on when AI agents join the org chart.

Investment Activity

Funding and M&A activity in AI agents accelerated in June, reflecting investor confidence despite the reliability concerns highlighted by research.

Coralogix debuted an AI agent after raising $115 million . Commure rolled out AI agents for healthcare workflow automation fresh off a $200 million raise .

Sema4.ai snagged $25 million for its AI agent platform, as confirmed by Axios . Veris AI emerged from stealth with $8.5 million to train AI agents using simulated experience. Sedai raised $20 million to optimize cloud environments with AI agents.

On the M&A front, Snyk acquired Invariant Labs to expand AI agent security capabilities. Rubrik acquired Predibase to scale AI agent development. Snowflake agreed to acquire Crunchy Data to strengthen its AI agent business.

Other investment developments included Sonos investing in agentic AI and CIO reporting AI agents were everywhere at the RSA Conference.

Developer & Coding Agents

New Tools

Research & Experiments

Experimental Deployments

Academic Research

MIT Technology Review questioned whether we’re ready to hand AI agents the keys. MIT also examined how AI agents can learn to reason like humans.

Several outlets published comprehensive explainers about AI agents. CNET explained what agentic AI is. Wavestone published an agentic AI playbook. RealEstateNews.com covered what to know about AI agents.

Use Cases and Examples

FutureScot provided a guide to leveraging AI agents for public services. Mashable listed seven popular AI agents widely used by companies. CIO outlined nine promising use cases for business.

NVIDIA showed how to scale realistic robot simulation using the NeMo Agent Toolkit for physical AI. AutoGPT listed 20 AI agent examples in 2025.

Industry Analysis

KDnuggets questioned if it’s too early or already behind for AI agents in analytics workflows. Salesforce Agentforce 3 coverage focused on visibility. Bernard Marr argued AI agents are the missing link between enterprise ambition and execution.

Interoperability & Standards

Efforts to standardize agent communication accelerated in June, aimed at preventing ecosystem fragmentation.

Google and the Linux Foundation pushed the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol to enable agent-to-agent communication. Towards Data Science explained the protocol’s design. TechRepublic reported that the vendor-neutral interoperability project’s participants include Microsoft, Google, AWS, and Salesforce. SDxCentral covered the open standard push.

Security concerns accompanied the interoperability push. TrendMicro warned that a classic MCP server vulnerability can undermine entire AI agent ecosystems.

IBM covered how AI agents collaborate and the world of multi-agent orchestration. Amazon Bedrock showed how to build an intelligent multi-agent business expert.

China’s AI Agent Boom

China’s AI agent ecosystem developed in parallel to Western efforts, with local companies launching distinct offerings.

MIT Technology Review reported that Manus has kick-started an AI agent boom in China. China Daily covered Laiye launching an enterprise-level AI agent matrix.

ZTE accelerated AI agent innovation with its AI Agent Factory Co-Sight solution. Caixin Global published an in-depth analysis describing AI agents as triggering the next tech battlefield in China.

Rest of World reported that China is gaining ground in the global race to develop AI agents. Yum China rolled out an AI agent to help rather than replace store managers.

Looking Ahead

June’s developments paint a complex picture of agentic AI’s trajectory. Platforms are launching rapidly, enterprises are investing heavily, and use cases are proliferating across industries. Yet the research reveals significant reliability gaps that must be addressed.

The Tension Between Hype and Reality

ZDNET argued AI agents will be ambient but not autonomous. VentureBeat suggested agent-based computing is outgrowing the web as we know it. Yet Bernard Marr highlighted five AI agent myths that need to be debunked.

Oracle positioned agentic AI as the next big thing in artificial intelligence, while CIO clarified how AI agents and agentic AI differ from each other.

Workforce Transformation

The workforce implications of AI agents received significant attention. TechRadar considered whether we’re ready to welcome AI agents as team members. Workday explored how AI agents are reshaping work, roles, and strategy. IT Brief Australia emphasized balancing innovation with responsibility.

McKinsey explored seizing the agentic AI advantage. Another McKinsey piece declared the future of work is agentic.

Strategic Guidance

For business leaders, CIO provided guidance on scaling AI agents for business. TechTarget examined AI agents as increasingly viable for enterprise use.

Substack covered the AI agent architecture debate. The AI Journal argued AI agents are the future of business process automation.

The Path Forward

The World Economic Forum suggested agentic AI will revolutionize business in the cognitive era. IBM examined when AI agents join the org chart.

The research from Carnegie Mellon, Stanford, Salesforce, and Gartner suggests that while agentic AI holds tremendous promise, current limitations are significant. The ~70% error rate on multi-step tasks, the 65% failure rate on multiturn CRM tasks, and Gartner’s prediction that 40% of projects will be scrapped by 2027 all point to the need for realistic expectations.

Yet the enterprise momentum is undeniable. RSM’s $1 billion commitment, the major platform launches from Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft, and the expanding use cases across industries all signal that organizations see enough value to continue investing despite the limitations.

Success in this environment will likely require: human oversight for high-risk workflows; clear use cases that match agent capabilities; realistic expectations about reliability; investment in observability and monitoring; and gradual scaling from low-risk to higher-risk applications.

The gap between platform marketing and proven capability remains significant. But as the research benchmarks improve and enterprises learn where agents can deliver real value versus where they cannot, the industry should move toward more mature implementations. The companies that succeed will be those that balance enthusiasm for the technology’s potential with clear-eyed assessment of its current limitations.

item.content:encoded:
May 2025 marked a turning point for AI agents. OpenAI launched Codex, a full-fledged coding agent. Google DeepMind unveiled AlphaEvolve, an algorithm-discovery agent that outperforms humans. Microsoft used its Build conference to position Windows as an “agent factory” and announced cross-platform collaboration protocols. Perhaps most tellingly, a new survey found 50% of tech companies have already adopted AI agentsup from near-zero a year ago. The race to build agentic systems is no longer theoreticalit’s happening now.

This comprehensive review covers 280 articles published between May 1 and May 31, 2025, surveying the rapid evolution of AI agents across enterprise adoption, platform launches, protocol standards, security concerns, and funding activity.

The numbers tell the story. Microsoft projects 1.3 billion AI agents will be in operation by 2028. Google’s AlphaEvolve matches the best existing solutions in 75% of cases and finds better solutions in 20% of cases. Enterprise adoption hit 50% in May, up from minimal levels a year ago. And investors poured $113.5M+ into agent infrastructure startups in May alonewith over $1.1B including adjacent acquisitions.

This isn’t hype. These are production deployments, real products, and serious investments. The question is no longer whether AI agents will matter, but which agents will win and how they’ll work together.

Platform Wars: Three Major Launches Shape the Agentic Landscape

The first half of May 2025 saw three product launches that may well define the next phase of AI. Within six days, Google, OpenAI, and Microsoft each unveiled major agentic systems. The timing wasn’t coordinatedthe competitive stakes are simply that high.

OpenAI Codex: The Coding Agent

On May 16, OpenAI introduced Codex , its first full-fledged AI agent for software development. Unlike previous coding assistants, Codex operates as a true agentit can write software features, fix bugs, and run tests in a distinct container that mirrors the developer’s environment.

The tool is built on codex-1, a fine-tuned variation of OpenAI’s o3 reasoning model trained using reinforcement learning on a wide range of coding tasks. Tasks can take anywhere from one to 30 minutes to complete, and Codex shows its thinking at every step along the way. Developers can include an “AGENTS.md” file in their repository to provide custom instructionskind of a README.md but for AI agents rather than humans.

Coverage was widespread. Bloomberg positioned Codex as OpenAI’s answer to competitors like Google and Anthropic in the coding agent space. The Wall Street Journal covered the launch as a significant product announcement. Fast Company noted this represents a shift from assistant to agent.

InfoWorld described how Codex can tackle multi-step coding tasks. SiliconANGLE covered the ChatGPT integration. ITPro analyzed the implications for software engineering.

The Decoder provided deeper analysis on what this means for autonomous AI agents in software development. DevOps.com explored how Codex could transform DevOps workflows.

OpenAI’s official announcement emphasized the agent’s ability to handle multi-step coding tasks autonomously. The company noted that “it still remains essential for users to manually review and validate all agent-generated code before integration and execution"a nod to security concerns.

Codex is available in research preview to ChatGPT Pro, Enterprise, and Team users, with generous access at no additional cost for the coming weeks before rate limits and new pricing are introduced. Plus and Edu support is coming later.

Google AlphaEvolve: The Algorithm Discovery Agent

Two days earlier, on May 14, Google DeepMind unveiled AlphaEvolve , an AI agent that uses the Gemini 2.0 family of large language models to discover new algorithms. This isn’t just a coding assistantit’s an algorithm discovery engine that can find solutions humans haven’t.

The agent scored 16,000 candidate solutions to find algorithms for multiplying 14 different sizes of matrices faster than any existing approachincluding improving on Google DeepMind’s own AlphaTensor record for four-by-four matrices. More impressively, AlphaEvolve solved matrix multiplication with numbers other than just 0s and 1s, making it applicable to real-world computations.

In testing across more than 50 types of math puzzles, AlphaEvolve matched the best existing solutions in 75% of cases and found better solutions in 20% of cases. These aren’t toy problemsthey include Fourier analysis (the math behind video streaming), the minimum overlap problem (an open problem in number theory proposed by Paul Erdos in 1955), and kissing numbers (a problem introduced by Isaac Newton with applications in cryptography).

MIT Technology Review provided comprehensive coverage, noting that Google has been using AlphaEvolve’s server allocation algorithm across all its data centers for more than a year. The algorithm freed up 0.7% of Google’s total computing resourcesa significant amount at Google’s scale.

SiliconANGLE covered the agent’s optimization for coding and math. MarkTechPost detailed the Gemini-powered approach. Hackster.io explained how it handles hard problems beyond just coding.

AlphaEvolve works by generating multiple blocks of code using Gemini 2.0 Flash (the fastest version), scoring them according to accuracy and efficiency metrics, then iteratively improving the best candidates. When stuck, it can call on Gemini 2.0 Pro for more powerful reasoning. Beyond matrix multiplication, AlphaEvolve has found applications in reducing TPU chip power consumption and even speeding up Gemini’s own training process.

Pushmeet Kohli, a vice president at Google DeepMind who leads its AI for Science teams, called it “a sort of super coding agent” that “actually produces a result that maybe nobody was aware of.”

The implications are significant. Jakob Moosbauer, a mathematician at the University of Warwick, noted that “AI is becoming a tool that will be essential in mathematics and computer science.”

Microsoft Build: Windows as an Agent Factory

Microsoft’s Build 2025 conference, running May 19-30, represented perhaps the most ambitious platform play of all three launches. The company isn’t just building an agentit’s retooling the entire PC operating system as an agent platform.

The company unveiled Windows AI Foundry , a comprehensive platform for building and deploying AI agents on Windows. In an interview with The Verge, Microsoft’s Jay Parikh described the company’s vision as building an AI “agent factory"one that could produce millions of specialized agents.

Microsoft expects 1.3 billion AI agents to be in operation by 2028. That’s not a typo1.3 billion agents. To get there, the company announced new agent customization and oversight features, including AI agents that can change Windows 11 settings raising questions about user control. Beebom reported that the AI agent is first rolling out to Copilot+ PCs.

ZDNET covered the new AI agent customization and oversight features announced at Build. CRN called it “the biggest news in AI, agents, Windows.”

InfoQ provided comprehensive coverage of Microsoft’s AI agent and platform updates. The official Microsoft Blog framed it as “the age of AI agents and building the open agentic web.”

Beyond the operating system, Microsoft’s Build announcements spanned the entire product portfolio:

For Enterprise Resource Planning:

  • New AI agent features in Dynamics 365 for ERP business processes were detailed by Microsoft

For Healthcare:

  • Multi-agent orchestration for cancer care management was announced
  • MobiHealthNews covered the AI agent orchestrator for cancer care coordination

For Cross-Platform Collaboration:

  • Reuters reported that Microsoft wants AI agents to work together and remember things
  • VentureBeat explained how Microsoft taught its AI agents to talk to each other

For Agent Development:

  • Microsoft introduced the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol for cross-platform agent communication (more on this in the protocols section)

The scope of Microsoft’s ambition is clearest in the official blog post , which declares “the age of AI agents” and promises “the open agentic web.” This isn’t just a product launchit’s a platform strategy aimed at making Windows the foundation for agentic computing.

The Broader Launch Landscape

Beyond the three major platform launches, May saw a wave of specialized agent announcements across every vertical. The breadth of announcements is staggeringagents for search, content operations, financial planning, trade surveillance, industrial automation, HR, legal, customer experience, and more.

Search and Content:

  • Algolia unveiled real-time, context-aware AI agents for Salesforce and Adobe
  • Box expanded its platform with AI agents for search, deep research, and data extraction . GeekWire covered how Box is tightening Microsoft ties with new Copilot integration
  • Hugging Face released a free Operator-like agentic AI tool , providing an open source alternative to proprietary agents
  • Contentsquare announced Sense , an AI agent that plans and acts like an analyst

Content Operations:

  • Aprimo launched AI agents for content operations
  • Smartpress debuted Smartpress Intelligence , its new AI agent for print operations

Enterprise Platforms:

  • SourceNow introduced Sage AI , the first AI agent built inside a VMS platform
  • Vena set a new standard in agentic AI for FP&A with Microsoft Teams integration
  • Saifr collaborated with Microsoft to deploy an AI agent for compliant content creation
  • Oracle introduced ASK Agent to revolutionize the Oracle B2C Service agent experience with AI

Financial Services:

  • Temenos launched an AI agent to transform financial crime mitigation
  • Solidus Labs launched an AI agent for trade surveillance
  • Salesforce targeted a more human touch for financial services firms with AI agents

HR and Workforce:

  • UKG and SAP SuccessFactors joined the rush to launch AI agents for HR
  • Microsoft explored how AI agents transform work in the Bay Area

Legal and Compliance:

  • Definely entered the legal AI agent race with a contract review tool
  • Greenlite AI secured $15M to scale trusted AI compliance agents

Industrial and Technical:

  • Siemens introduced AI agents for industrial automation
  • Scrypted acquired Chibi Clash to advance AI agent-powered gaming

Customer Experience and Contact Centers:

  • **Voice AI agents are redefining CX](https://opusresearch.net/2025/05/19/voice-ai-agents-redefine-cx-trends-roi-and-strategies-for-2025/) , with a comprehensive look at trends, ROI, and strategies
  • SoundHound launched Amelia 7.0 , delivering agentic AI with category-leading voice technology
  • Soul Machines partnered with ServiceNow to bring experiential AI agents to the ServiceNow Store

Blockchain and Crypto:

  • Nimanode launched the first AI agent platform on XRP Ledger
  • Fox 5 San Diego covered how Nimanode is pioneering no-code AI agents on XRP

Regional and Industry Developments:

  • Mexico Business News explored the rise of AI agents in Mexico’s workforce
  • Latenode launched an AI agent node to automate customer-facing workflows

The competitive dynamic is clear: three tech giants placing different bets on what agents should do, while a wave of startups and incumbents launch specialized agents for every vertical. This isn’t a winner-take-all marketit’s a transformation of how software works across the board.

The Enterprise Adoption Wave: 50% and Rising

Adoption by the Numbers

The headline statistic comes from an Inc.com survey : 50% of tech companies report adopting AI agentsup from minimal adoption just a year ago. This isn’t pilot programs anymorethese are production deployments.

Nasscom predicts that agents will drive the next wave of enterprise transformation in 2025. The industry organization’s analysis frames agents as the next major enterprise technology wave, comparable to cloud computing or mobile.

Microsoft’s Work Trend Index found workforce and leadership aligning on intelligent agent integration. The study, focused on Malaysia but indicative of global trends, found both employees and executives recognizing the potential of AI agents to transform work.

The momentum is global. A study from the University of St. George’s found that groups of AI agents spontaneously form their own social norms without human helpraising questions about how autonomous agent swarms will behave in enterprise settings. The research suggests that multi-agent systems may develop emergent behaviors that aren’t explicitly programmed.

GenerativX explored how to tailor AI agents to enterprise finance’s needs, noting the importance of domain-specific customization.

Major Enterprise Deployments

The big consultancies and enterprise software companies are moving aggressively. This isn’t “wait and see"these are production announcements and GA launches.

Consulting and Services:

  • Infosys launched over 200 enterprise AI agents as part of its Topaz AI offerings, developed in collaboration with Google Cloud. The scale of the launch200+ distinct agentsindicates how deeply Infosys is embedding AI across its service lines
  • Deloitte is integrating Zora AI with SAP Joule agents to unlock deep reasoning capabilities. The partnership shows how traditional consulting firms are becoming AI system integrators

Enterprise Software Giants:

  • IBM unveiled Agent Connect , a new marketplace for enterprise AI agents. The company is leaning on agents to scale execution across the enterprise, as covered at IBM Think 2025. AI Business reported on IBM’s tools to accelerate AI agent adoption
  • IBM Research published findings on AI agents’ impact across org structures
  • ServiceNow and NVIDIA partnered to fuel a new class of intelligent AI agents. SiliconANGLE explored how an agent workforce could be on the horizon, with ServiceNow and Accenture discussing the implications
  • Box announced an all-new AI platform to bring powerful AI agents to enterprise content
  • Glean unveiled a scalable AI agent platform for the enterprise. Channel Insider covered Glean’s expansion of its AI agent environment
  • NTT DATA launched an AI agent ecosystem to support enterprise automation
  • Workday added seven new AI agents to its cloud platform, expanding its agentic capabilities for HR and finance
  • SAP announced plans to make its Joule AI agent omnipresent at Sapphire 2025

Partnerships:

  • IBM and Oracle expanded their partnership to advance agentic AI and hybrid cloud
  • Carvana built an efficient customer experience with an agent on Azure, as detailed in a Microsoft customer story

Industry-Specific Enterprise Tools

Enterprises are deploying agents for specialized workflows, with industry-specific customization becoming increasingly important:

Financial Planning and Analysis (FP&A):

  • Vena set a new standard in agentic AI for FP&A with Microsoft Teams integration
  • OneStream shook up its finance software portfolio with AI agents

Healthcare:

  • SoundHound AI and Allina Health launched an AI agent to redefine patient engagement
  • Google rolled out AI travel agents that can plan trips far beyond “assistant” status, as CNBC reported

  • Temenos launched an AI agent to transform financial crime mitigation

  • Block (Jack Dorsey’s company) made an AI agent to boost its own productivity, showcasing dogfooding of agent technology

Data and Analytics:

  • S&P Global’s AI chief discussed the ’exciting’ pace of agentic AI innovation

Regional Development:

  • Mexico Business News explored the rise of AI agents in Mexico’s workforce, highlighting global adoption patterns

Monitoring and Orchestration

As enterprises deploy more agents, monitoring and orchestration become critical. You can’t manage what you can’t measure, and you can’t orchestrate what you can’t observe.

Monitoring Platforms:

  • Patronus AI debuted Percival , a tool for fixing AI agent malfunctions. VentureBeat explained how Percival helps enterprises monitor failing AI agents at scalea critical capability as production deployments increase

Orchestration Platforms:

  • Azure AI Foundry Agent Service went GA with multi-agent orchestration capabilities. InfoQ covered the GA announcement in detail
  • Azure Logic Apps introduced Agent Loop for building AI agents in enterprise workflows, providing a visual way to orchestrate agent interactions
  • Amazon Bedrock introduced multi-agent collaboration for investment research, showing how specialized agents can collaborate on complex tasks
  • A VentureBeat analysis explored how architectural design drives reliable multi-agent orchestration , emphasizing the importance of system design

Orchestrator Evaluation:

  • Constellation Research explored how to pick an AI agent orchestrator when every vendor wants to be yoursa growing challenge as the market fragments

The emergence of monitoring and orchestration as distinct categories indicates that AI agents are moving from experiments to production systems. Enterprises need observability, control, and governancejust like any other production technology.

The Standards Battle: Agent Communication Protocols Emerge

The Protocol Landscape

May 2025 saw the emergence of a standards battle reminiscent of early internet protocols. The stakes are high: without standards, agents from different vendors can’t communicate, leading to fragmented silos rather than an interoperable agentic web.

Microsoft’s adoption of Google’s A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol is the most significant signal. Microsoft announced support for the open protocol on May 7a notable move given the companies’ usual competition. YourStory covered Microsoft’s adoption of Google’s AI agent protocol and why it matters.

Computerworld described Google’s AI agent protocol as becoming “the language for digital labor"a phrase that captures the economic significance of this infrastructure work.

IBM’s counter-move came on May 28, when the company announced an open-source protocol for AI agents to interact. IBM’s entry adds another contender to the mix and underscores that the protocol battle is still in early stages.

Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) is also gaining traction:

  • PwC added support for MCP in its agent OS
  • Apollo GraphQL launched an MCP server as a gateway between AI agents and enterprise APIs

Microsoft’s MCP Rollouts expanded significantly:

  • Cloudwars covered Microsoft’s major push into AI agent interoperability with new MCP rollouts

Why Protocols Matter

Agents need to talk to each other to be useful at scale. A travel agent needs to talk to airline booking systems. A research agent needs to talk to databases and APIs. Without standards, every agent becomes an isolated walled garden.

Microsoft is pushing for cross-company AI agent collaboration to boost workforce efficiency. The company recognizes that agents from different organizations need to work together.

Towards Data Science proposed ACP: The Internet Protocol for AI Agentsa more ambitious approach that would create a true protocol layer for agentic communication.

The tech community is exploring DNS-like infrastructure:

  • The Register covered the proposal for Agent Name Servicelike DNS but for AI agents

This is infrastructure work that will determine whether agents become interoperable or siloed. The next 6-12 months will likely see shakeout in the protocol space, with one or two standards emerging as dominant. The question is: which protocol becomes the standard?

The Dark Side: Security Risks and Reliability Concerns

As adoption accelerates, security concerns are growing proportionally. The more agents enterprises deploy, the more attack surface and failure modes emerge. May 2025 saw extensive coverage of these risksand the emerging solutions.

Novel Failure Modes

Rapid adoption is creating new risks. AI agents can fail in novel ways that businesses don’t expect. They may have memory problems , forgetting critical context that humans would remember.

A viral experiment showed AI agents looking after a vending machine and “going completely mad” . The agents developed unexpected behaviors that weren’t programmedillustrating how autonomous systems can behave unpredictably in real-world environments.

Microsoft’s announcement that its agents can change Windows 11 settings created a “delight or terror” dilemma. The convenience of automation comes with loss of control. BetaNews asked whether we should be delighted or terrifieda question that captures the ambivalence many feel about autonomous agents.

The Register reported that AI agents are confused by some aspects of websites and ads, highlighting technical challenges agents face in navigating the web as humans do.

Data Security Threats

The security risks are proportional to adoption. Axios reported on AI agents “going rogue” as a new cybersecurity risk. Because agents have access to sensitive data and systems, they represent “keys to the kingdom” for attackers.

A survey found that AI agents pose rising security risks for firms. Security Magazine noted that as agentic AI becomes everywhere, so do the security risks.

Trend Micro published a series of analyses on agent vulnerabilities:

  • AI agent database access vulnerabilities
  • Securing LLM services

Reliability Solutions

The industry is developing solutions to address these challenges:

Guardian Agents:

  • VentureBeat described how “guardian agents” could reduce AI hallucinations below 1% an approach that uses one agent to monitor another. This “agent watching agents” pattern is emerging as a key reliability strategy

Enterprise Security:

  • Vectra AI broadened its AI agents to bolster cybersecurity for customers, using agents to fight agent-based threats
  • Check Point published analysis on AI agents and the future of cyber security
  • Zenity enhanced security from buildtime to runtime for enterprise AI agents with Copilot Studio

Enterprise Trust:

  • Salesforce announced initiatives to bring trust and governance to AI agents
  • CIOs are taking note. Alvarez & Marsal asked whether enterprises are ready for the security challenges
  • Harvard Business Review explored whether AI agents can be trusted

Definition and Readiness Questions

There’s also a fundamental question: what even is an AI agent?

As TechCrunch reported, even a16z VCs say no one really knows . This definitional uncertainty makes it hard to assess readiness, benchmark performance, or even have coherent conversations about the technology.

A PYMNTS study asked whether AI agents are ready to take over human work and found: not yet. The gap between hype and reality remains significant.

One analysis examined the difference between AI agents and agentic AI , trying to separate signal from noise in the boom.

Legal Liability:

  • Wired explored who’s to blame when AI agents screw upa legal gray area that courts and regulators are only beginning to address

Hype vs Reality:

  • Alvarez & Marsal published a guide on demystifying AI agents in 2025, separating hype from reality and navigating market outlook

Enterprise Trust Survey:

  • PwC conducted an AI agent survey examining enterprise adoption and trust issues

The security and reliability concerns aren’t deal-breakers, but they’re real. Enterprises deploying agents need monitoring tools, governance frameworks, and security strategiesjust like any other production technology. The difference is that agents are autonomous, which makes traditional security models less effective. New approaches are needed.

Market Activity: Funding Flows to Agent Infrastructure

Notable Funding Rounds

May 2025 saw substantial investment in agent infrastructure, with significant rounds across seed, Series B, and growth stages:

  • Relevance AI raised $24M Series B to help anyone build teams of AI agents. PYMNTS covered how the funds will grow the AI agent operating system
  • Coworker.ai raised $13M seed for the first AI agent with deep company context, bringing total funding to $16.5M. The round was led by Jeff Huber, former SVP of Google Ads, Maps, and Workspace

Acquisitions and Strategic Moves

M&A activity is also heating up as established companies acquire agent capabilities:

  • Databricks announced plans to buy Neon for $1 billion to boost AI agent development. The Business Times confirmed the $1 billion price tag
  • Alation acquired Numbers Station to expand AI agent capabilities for enterprise data workflows
  • Nimanode launched the first AI agent platform on XRP Ledger, combining blockchain infrastructure with agent capabilities
  • Salesforce announced an $8B Informatica buy as AI agents take shape, doubling down on data infrastructure

Infrastructure Investment

Major cloud providers are investing heavily in agent infrastructure:

  • Microsoft announced an Agent Store marketplace , positioning itself as the platform for agent distribution
  • Microsoft made major pushes into AI agent interoperability with new MCP rollouts

The Billion-Dollar Question

ZDNET asked whether you can build a billion-dollar business with only AI agentsand concluded yes. The question isn’t if agent businesses can scale, but which business models will win.

Total May funding tracked for dedicated agent infrastructure: $113.5M+ across major rounds. This doesn’t include adjacent rounds for AI companies adding agent capabilities, or the massive Databricks/Neon acquisition. If we include the $1B Neon acquisition, May saw over $1.1B in agent-related deal flow.

The investment patterns show where the market sees opportunity: agent infrastructure (Relevance AI), vertical specialization (Samaya AI), compliance (Greenlite AI), and developer tools (TensorStax). These aren’t generic AI companiesthey’re focused on the agent category specifically.

Agent Applications: From Healthcare to Crypto Browsers

The breadth of AI agent applications emerging in May 2025 is extraordinary. This isn’t a single technology being applied in one wayit’s a new paradigm being applied across every sector of the economy. From quantum chemistry to credit card transactions, from cancer care to crypto trading, agents are being deployed everywhere.

Healthcare & Mental Health

Healthcare is emerging as a major use case for AI agents, and the applications are getting more sophisticated:

  • Pager Health rolled out a new AI agent to guide health plan members through wellness programs
  • Google Research published on AMIE , a research AI agent for multimodal diagnostic dialogue with vision capabilities. The agent can now process images alongside text, making it more versatile for medical diagnosis
  • Microsoft unveiled an AI agent orchestrator for cancer care , showing how multi-agent systems can coordinate complex treatment pathways

Biopharma and Drug Discovery:

Browsers & User Interfaces

The web browser is becoming an agent platform, potentially transforming how we interact with the web:

  • Donut is building an AI agent crypto browser as a challenger to Brave and Opera, focused specifically on cryptocurrency interactions
  • Google announced that its AI agents will bring you the web a fundamental shift from browsing to being served
  • Google rolled out Project Mariner , its web-browsing AI agent that can navigate websites autonomously
  • PYMNTS asked whether AI agents are coming for Chrome, Safari, and how we surf the webconcluding that the browser itself may need to be reimagined for an agentic future

E-Commerce and Shopping:

Developer & Scientific Tools

Scientific and developer tools are rapidly adding agent capabilities, potentially transforming how research and development happen:

Payments and Fintech

The payments industry is grappling with how agents will change financial transactions:

  • Andreessen Horowitz published How Will My Agent Pay for Things? , exploring the agent payments stack and how financial infrastructure needs to evolve
  • American Banker argued that a future full of AI agents will require a different payments system

Marketing and Advertising

Marketing and advertising are seeing early agent adoption:

  • The Register noted that AI agents are confused by some aspects of websites and ads, highlighting challenges for agent-driven advertising

Hospitality and Travel

The travel and hospitality industry is exploring agent applications:

  • Another Hospitality Net piece explored how AI agents will reshape hospitality business processes
  • CNBC covered how AI travel agents are planning trips far beyond “assistant” status

Gaming and Entertainment

Gaming is an emerging frontier for AI agents:

  • Scrypted acquired Chibi Clash to advance AI agent-powered gaming

Experiments & Edge Cases

May also saw unusual experiments that tested agent boundaries:

  • Firecrawl, a Y Combinator startup, offered to pay $1M to hire three AI agents as employeesa provocative experiment in agent-as-employee
  • The vending machine experiment showed agents “going completely mad” , illustrating how agents can behave unpredictably in physical environments
  • A study found that groups of AI agents spontaneously form their own social normsa fascinating glimpse at emergent behavior
  • Stanford HAI published research on simulating human behavior with AI agents

Infrastructure Platforms

Major infrastructure announcements showed the maturation of the agent ecosystem:

  • Boomi leapt on the agentic AI boom , reporting 33,000 AI agents deployed. Constellation Research covered Boomi World 2025, noting Agentstudio, AWS pact, and 33,000 AI agents deployed
  • The Boomi CEO warned that “you will fail” without a governance plan in the agent era
  • ServiceNow and Accenture explored the agent workforce horizon
  • Siemens introduced AI agents for industrial automation
  • Workday added seven new AI agents to its cloud platform
  • SAP announced plans to make its Joule AI agent omnipresent at Sapphire 2025

China and Global Markets

The agent revolution is global:

  • South China Morning Post reported that China’s Manus AI makes registration free amid increasing AI agent competition

This breadth of applications shows that AI agents aren’t a single technology or use case. They’re a new way of building softwareautonomous, goal-directed systems that can operate across domains. The diversity of applications suggests we’re still in the early days of discovering what’s possible.

Looking Ahead: What May 2025 Means for the Future of Agents

The Mainstream Moment

Three major platform launches from OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft show that agentic systems are now a strategic priority for Big Tech. These aren’t research projectsthey’re product announcements with GA dates, pricing plans, and enterprise features. Codex is in research preview but rolling out broadly. AlphaEvolve is already deployed in Google’s data centers. Windows AI Foundry is being integrated into the world’s most widely-used operating system.

The 50% enterprise adoption rate suggests we’re past the early adopter phase. When half of tech companies are using a technology, it’s moved from experimental to operational. This isn’t “the next big thing” anymoreit’s the current thing.

Microsoft’s projection of 1.3 billion agents by 2028 is perhaps the most striking number. If accurate, we’re looking at a world where agents outnumber humans. That’s not just a technology shiftit’s an economic and social transformation.

The Infrastructure Phase

The protocol standards battleA2A versus MCP versus IBM’s open protocolindicates the field is maturing. Infrastructure is being built. This is typical of technology adoption: first come point solutions, then platforms, then standards.

The question for the next 6-12 months is interoperability: can agents from different vendors work together? The protocol battle will determine whether we get an open agentic web or walled gardens.

Computerworld’s description of agent protocols as “the language for digital labor” captures the stakes. We’re not just building softwarewe’re defining how autonomous systems will coordinate economic activity. The protocol winners could become as foundational as TCP/IP was to the internet.

The Open Questions

Despite the momentum, significant questions remain:

Definition clarity: Even VCs at a16z acknowledge no one knows what an AI agent is. This definitional uncertainty creates confusion in the market. Is a chatbot an agent? Is a scheduled script an agent? Without clear definitions, it’s hard to measure adoption or compare solutions.

Business models: Can you build a scalable business with only AI agents? The $113.5M+ in May funding (plus the $1B Databricks/Neon acquisition) says investors think so. But proven models at scale are rare. The agent-as-employee model (Firecrawl offering to pay agents) and the agent-platform model (Microsoft’s “agent factory”) are very different bets on how value accrues.

Security and reliability: Novel failure modes, rogue agents, and data access concerns are growing proportionally to adoption. The guardian agent approachusing agents to monitor agentsis promising but adds complexity. At what point do we have more agents monitoring agents than agents doing actual work?

Legal liability: Who’s responsible when agents screw up? The Wired piece on liability issues barely scratched the surface. When an autonomous agent makes a decision that causes harm, is the developer liable? The deployer? The user? The agent itself? Legal frameworks haven’t caught up with the technology.

Human readiness: A PYMNTS study found consumers aren’t sold on agents for credit card transactions. Trust takes time to build. The technology may be ready before humans are.

The Outlook

May 2025 may be remembered as the month AI agents went mainstream. The diversity of applications280+ articles across healthcare, finance, coding, browsers, content operationsshows agents aren’t one product but a new computing paradigm being applied everywhere.

The next phase will be about:

  • Interoperability: Can agents from different vendors work together?
  • Governance: How do we control autonomous systems?
  • Measurement: How do we define and measure agent performance?
  • Trust: How do we build confidence in agent decisions?

The hype is real, but so are the challenges. Enterprises deploying agents need:

  • Monitoring tools like Patronus AI’s Percival
  • Governance platforms like what Salesforce announced
  • Security strategies like what CIOs are discussing
  • Orchestration capabilities like what Azure and AWS are building

The race to build agentic systems is no longer theoretical. It’s happening now, and May 2025 was the month the race truly began.

The winners won’t necessarily be the companies with the best algorithms. They’ll be the ones who figure out reliability, trust, and governance at scale. They’ll be the ones who build the platforms that make agents useful rather than scary. They’ll be the ones who navigate the regulatory and liability landscapes that are just starting to take shape.

We’re still early. The protocol battle hasn’t been won. The business models aren’t proven. The legal frameworks don’t exist. But the direction is clear: agents are becoming a fundamental part of how software works and how work gets done.

May 2025 didn’t invent AI agents. But it may have marked the moment they became inevitable.

Google dropped A2A, an open protocol for AI agents to talk to each other. Microsoft says every worker will soon be an “agent boss” managing AI teammates alongside human colleagues. Visa and Mastercard are preparing for AI shopping agents. Meanwhile, CIOs are asking: Is this real or just hype?

This comprehensive review covers 185 articles published in April 2025, surveying the rapidly evolving AI agent landscape. Major tech firms unveiled competing visions for how autonomous AI will transform enterprise work, protocol wars emerged, and security partnerships formed to address enterprise concerns.

The Protocol Wars Begin

The most significant technical development of April was Google’s launch of A2A (Agent-to-Agent), an open protocol designed to enable AI agents to communicate directly with each other. Announced on April 9 , A2A addresses a fundamental bottleneck in multi-agent systems: interoperability.

The protocol allows AI agents from different developers and platforms to exchange information and coordinate actions without requiring custom integrations for each pair of systems. This is the foundational infrastructure needed for multi-agent workflows to scale beyond single-vendor ecosystems. As The Stack reported , Google’s announcement immediately sparked a “protocol war” with competing standards.

The competitive landscape includes:

  • A2A (Agent-to-Agent): Google’s open protocol for universal agent communication
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): Anthropic’s protocol for connecting AI models to external data sources
  • ACP (Agent Communication Protocol): An alternative approach from other vendors

The emergence of multiple competing standards reflects the high stakes. The protocol that achieves broad adoption will shape how agents interact for years to come. Vendors are positioning their protocols as the foundation for enterprise agent ecosystems.

Google complemented the A2A announcement with new agent building tools and an open source framework added to Vertex AI for building agents. These tools give developers practical ways to implement A2A in their applications.

Enterprise interest in agent interoperability is real. TCS partnered with Google Cloud on A2A interoperability to help enterprises build “future-ready” agent systems. The partnership signals that large systems integrators are already preparing to implement agent-to-agent communication for their clients.

The protocol question remains unresolved. Which standard will win? The answer may come down to which vendor can attract the most developer adoption and enterprise partnerships. Google’s first-mover advantage with A2A is significant, but Anthropic’s MCP has gained traction through its integration with popular AI models. The next few months will be critical in determining which protocol becomes the de facto standard for agent communication.

Microsoft’s Agent Boss Future

Microsoft made its clearest statement yet on AI agents in April: every human worker will soon be an “agent boss” , managing AI teammates alongside human colleagues. This isn’t framed as incremental productivity improvement—it’s presented as an org chart transformation.

The vision comes from Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index, which highlights how AI agents are reshaping the future of work . Microsoft envisions a workplace where each employee manages a team of AI agents, with human-to-agent ratios becoming a critical metric for organizational success. As Constellation Research reported , these ratios “will be critical to success as new roles emerge.”

The practical implementation involves several new capabilities:

Azure AI Foundry received new capabilities for building advanced agentic applications . The platform now provides unified tooling for developing, deploying, and managing AI agents at enterprise scale. These enhancements aim to simplify the journey from prototype to production for agentic systems.

Agent flows were introduced as a new concept for transforming automation with AI-first workflows . Agent flows provide a visual way to design multi-step workflows where AI agents coordinate with each other and with humans to complete complex tasks.

The Copilot Control System was announced to bring “order and management” to potential AI agent sprawl. As enterprises deploy dozens or hundreds of agents, managing them becomes a challenge—similar to the API sprawl problem of previous decades. The control system provides centralized governance.

Microsoft also announced three new AI agents for autonomous contact centers , targeting customer service as a key use case. These agents can handle routine inquiries, route complex issues to humans, and learn from interactions over time.

Customer deployments show the vision in practice. NTT DATA is transforming its enterprise with agentic AI in Microsoft Fabric and Azure AI Foundry. Roland Berger relies on AI agents and Microsoft Azure to create “more time for value creation.”

Microsoft’s broader messaging frames agentic AI as driving AI-first business transformation . The company’s research division also published on how human-agent teams will reshape the workforce .

Not everyone accepts the “agent boss” framing uncritically. As CIO.com explored , Microsoft sees AI agents shaking up org charts and eliminating traditional functions—but The Guardian noted the uncertainty around what this means for workers. Geekwire characterized the shift as Microsoft seeing “humans as ‘agent bosses,’ upending the workplace.”

Additional Microsoft announcements included new computer use capabilities in Copilot Studio for UI automation, guidance on identifying readiness for AI-first development , and a report on agents of change unlocking potential .

Microsoft also tapped AI agents and partners to scale and automate cybersecurity protections, extending the agentic vision into security operations.

The Great Platform Rush

Google wasn’t the only company building agent infrastructure in April. A wave of platform announcements from major vendors revealed a land grab for developer mindshare.

Google’s Double Play

Beyond the A2A protocol, Google announced the Agent Development Kit , which lets enterprises “rapidly prototype and deploy AI agents without recoding.” The kit provides pre-built components and templates to accelerate agent development.

Google Cloud also unveiled an AI Agent Marketplace at its Next conference, creating a centralized location for discovering and deploying pre-built agents. The marketplace approach mirrors the app store model, aiming to create an ecosystem around Google’s agent platform.

Nvidia Goes GA

Nvidia announced the general availability of NeMo tools for building AI agents . The NeMo Microservices are designed to create an “AI agent data flywheel”—as agents interact with systems, they generate data that can improve future agent performance.

Nvidia also unveiled the AI-Q Blueprint for transforming AI agent systems into digital workforces, and published technical content on building enterprise AI agents with advanced open Llama Nemotron reasoning models.

Enterprise Governance

Dataiku introduced AI Agents to unify and govern enterprise agent deployments . The focus on governance reflects enterprise concerns about managing agent sprawl, ensuring compliance, and maintaining oversight as agents proliferate.

**Futurum Group analyzed Oracle’s AI Agent Studio](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/is-oracles-ai-agent-studio-the-missing-layer-for-enterprise-wide-automation/) , positioning it as “the missing layer for enterprise-wide automation.” Oracle’s approach emphasizes unified management and integration with existing enterprise systems.

Other Platform Announcements

  • Writer unveiled “AI HQ” as a platform betting on agents to transform enterprise work
  • Amazon Web Services published on building multi-agent systems with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock
  • Camunda added AI agents to its process orchestration platform

Security: Agents as Threat and Shield

AI agents are reshaping cybersecurity in two directions—agents are being deployed to defend against threats, but they’re also creating new attack vectors.

Defensive Agents

Security vendors are rapidly incorporating agents into their products:

Vectra AI completed its groundbreaking agent portfolio , positioning its agentic AI systems as “setting new standard” for threat detection and security team efficiency.

Abnormal AI launched breakthrough AI agents to reimagine security awareness training and provide instant board-ready data insights. The agents aim to automate security training while providing executives with visibility into security posture.

Jit launched AI agents to ease AppSec workload , bringing automation to application security testing.

Nvidia published on advancing cybersecurity operations with agentic AI systems and how agentic AI enables the next leap in cybersecurity .

Google, Radiant, and Qevlar expanded AI agent use for SOCs (security operations centers).

Solutions Review catalogued the top AI agents for cybersecurity teams .

Securing the Agents

As agents become more powerful, securing them becomes critical:

CyberArk and Accenture partnered to secure enterprise AI agents . The partnership combines CyberArk’s identity security with Accenture’s AI Refinery to address what CyberArk calls identity security for AI agents .

Sentra introduced Data Security for AI Agents as a solution to secure the next generation of business automation .

TechTarget explored how AI agents raise stakes in identity and access management .

CIO Dive reported that IT leaders want better security and data privacy from AI agents.

New Attack Vectors

MIT Technology Review warned that cyberattacks by AI agents are coming . The article explores how autonomous AI could be used to conduct more sophisticated, adaptive cyberattacks at scale.

CFO Dive noted that AI agents emerge as potential targets for cyberattackers—a new threat vector where attackers compromise agents themselves to gain access to enterprise systems.

Company Security Focus Approach
CyberArk + Accenture Identity Security Partnership
Vectra AI Threat Detection AI-Powered Agents
Abnormal AI Security Training Awareness Agents
Sentra Data Security Agent Protection
Jit AppSec Workload Automation

Shopping With AI Agents

E-commerce is quietly becoming the first major battleground for practical AI agent applications.

Amazon’s new AI agent will shop third-party sites for you . The agent browses external websites to find products, compare prices, and make purchases—extending Amazon’s reach beyond its own marketplace.

Mastercard’s Agent Pay transforms how enterprises use AI search by eliminating window switching. The product enables AI agents to complete purchases directly within enterprise workflows, removing friction between search and transaction.

Visa gives AI shopping agents “intelligent commerce ” capabilities by extending its payment rails to support agent-initiated transactions. AP News reported that Visa “wants to give artificial intelligence ‘agents’ your credit card.”

Visa CMO Frank Cooper III discussed the company’s bet on AI agents in an interview about “culture, commerce and marketing’s next frontier.”

Nvidia explored how AI agents enhance online shopping , outlining use cases for personalized recommendations, automated comparison shopping, and conversational commerce.

These developments point to a future where AI agents become primary participants in e-commerce—representing consumers in transactions, negotiating prices, and making purchasing decisions. The payment networks’ early positioning suggests they see agents as both an opportunity and a threat to existing commerce models.

Healthcare’s Agent Experiment

Healthcare emerged in April as a key early adopter of AI agent technology, with several focused deployments in high-value use cases.

Infinitus launched the first trusted voice AI agents for healthcare , targeting administrative workflows like prior authorization and benefits verification.

Cedar rolled out an AI voice agent to tackle patients’ medical billing questions , addressing a major pain point in healthcare finance.

Seattle Children’s teamed up with Google Cloud to develop a decision-support AI agent for healthcare providers. The clinical decision support agent aims to help clinicians access relevant information more quickly.

Google Cloud sees multi-agent AI systems as healthcare’s “next frontier” , expanding AI agent tools for healthcare .

Oracle reported that AI agents show promise in transforming healthcare .

PwC explored how Google Cloud and AI agents transform healthcare .

Relatient launched Dash Voice AI Agent to automate patient appointment management in call centers .

eHealth introduced AI voice agents to enhance customer experience in health plan selection .

Healthcare’s adoption pattern is notable: providers are focusing agents on administrative tasks (billing, appointments, prior authorization) rather than clinical decision-making. This reflects both regulatory caution and practical opportunity—healthcare has significant administrative overhead that agents can address without requiring clinical validation.

Workforce: Hype vs Reality

The hype machine surrounding AI agents reached new levels in April, even as enterprises struggled with basic questions about what AI agents actually are and how to deploy them.

The Reality Check

ZDNet reported that 60% of AI agents work in IT departments . The finding suggests that despite the hype about agents transforming every business function, actual deployment is heavily concentrated in technical functions.

CIO.com explored how CIOs struggle with the definition of what makes a true AI agent. The terminology confusion—chatbots vs. copilots vs. agents vs. agentic AI—creates challenges for procurement and evaluation.

SiliconANGLE examined the long road to agentic AI , contrasting hype with enterprise reality.

HR Executive asked whether AI agent implementation has stalled and whether HR can propel it forward.

Actuia considered whether 2025 is the year of maturity for enterprise AI agents.

Cutting Through the Hype

Salesforce introduced a 5-level framework for AI agents that cuts through the hype . The framework provides maturity levels to help enterprises distinguish between basic automation and true agentic systems.

UiPath AI agents blend with RPA amid industry hype and doubts , suggesting a more incremental evolution than revolutionary change.

Digiday profiled Salesforce’s transformation from CRM giant to “digital labor” provider , exploring how the company aims to “stand above the hype” with agentic AI.

Cautionary Tales

A company apologized after its AI support agent invented a policy that caused user uproar. The incident highlights the risks of autonomous agents making statements or commitments beyond their authority—a governance challenge that enterprises must address.

Professors staffed a fake company entirely with AI agents in an experiment covered by Futurism and DIGIT . The results were mixed, showing both promise and limitation in current agent capabilities.

Who’s Interested?

ZDNet analyzed the 4 types of people interested in AI agents and what businesses can learn from them.

Socradar asked whether AI agents are hype or reality .

NetworkWorld explored the distinction between AI agents vs. agentic AI and what enterprises actually want.

Market Signals: Funding and Startups

Venture capital activity and startup moves provide signals about where the market is placing bets:

  • Artisan raises $25M with a provocative “stop hiring humans” pitch —though the startup is still hiring humans itself
  • a16z backs UK startup Dex to scale an “AI talent agent” and recruitment matchmaker
  • Model ML seeks to acquire AI agent companies according to its CEO
  • A new agency is staffed with more AI agents than people and wants to keep it that way , according to Ad Age
  • Make launched Make AI Agents to add real-time intelligence to no-code automation

The funding pattern suggests investors are targeting specific horizontal use cases (recruitment, automation) rather than general-purpose agent platforms. The “stop hiring humans” framing generates attention, but the reality is more nuanced—companies are hiring humans to build and manage agents.

Developer Experience: Agents That Code

Software development remains a key use case for AI agents:

  • Augment Code launched Augment Agent as an AI pair programmer that deeply understands codebases and learns as you work
  • Microsoft Research published on Debug-gym exploring whether AI agents can lighten developers’ debugging load
  • DevOps.com explored how AI agents are reshaping the developer experience
  • Anthropic shared best practices for Claude Code agentic coding
  • Augment Code published how to prompt your agent with 8 tips and best practices for using AI coding agents

Coding agents benefit from clear evaluation criteria (does the code work?) and continuous feedback loops from integrated development environments. This makes them one of the more mature agent categories.

Industry Snapshot

AI agents are spreading across industries:

  • Adobe is building AI agents for Photoshop and Premiere Pro , including an agent that can show you how to use Photoshop
  • OneTrack launched AiOn as the first AI agent platform for autonomous logistics operations
  • MineOS unveiled an AI agent to transform data privacy management
  • SK Telecom touted AI agent ‘Aster’ as the future of telecom innovation
  • Atlassian shared customer impressions of putting the Rovo AI agent to work
  • Baidu rolled out new AI agent Xinxiang for Android
  • KPMG reported that most companies are just test-driving AI agents
  • Microsoft explored how AI and intelligent agents are transforming local government
  • Real estate and travel industries explored agents for homebuyers and vacation planning
  • Counterpoint Research analyzed how smartphone OEMs can stay competitive in the era of AI agents
  • Computer Weekly explored how AI agents will reshape telecoms

Looking Ahead: What April Means for Agents

April 2025 was a foundational month for AI agents. The developments weren’t incremental—they were structural changes to how agents will be built, deployed, and managed in enterprises.

The protocol wars (A2A vs MCP vs ACP) will determine how agents interoperate. No standard has won yet, and fragmentation is likely to persist in the near term. Enterprises should prepare for multi-protocol environments.

The “agent boss” vision from Microsoft represents one possible future for work—humans managing teams of AI agents. But other vendors envision different models (human-AI collaboration, agents as assistants rather than subordinates). The org chart of the future is still being negotiated.

Security partnerships like CyberArk + Accenture address what could be a blocking issue for enterprise adoption. If agents can’t be secured, they won’t be deployed. The emergence of specialized agent security offerings suggests the market is taking this seriously.

Healthcare and commerce are leading use cases with clear ROI and relatively lower regulatory barriers. These industries provide a preview of how agents will transform workflows in other sectors.

The hype is real, but so are the challenges. CIOs struggle with definitions. Implementation has stalled in some places. Early failures like the policy-inventing agent show the risks. According to ZDnet, 60% of AI agents work in IT departments—suggesting transformation is concentrated, not universal.

The market is moving from “what are agents?” to “which platform and protocol win?” Expect the protocol war to intensify, security offerings to multiply, and enterprises to run more pilots. The next six months will determine whether 2025 is the year agents mature—or another hype cycle peak.
